ques: what are your songwriting procedures and processes?
answ: 2 totally separate departments are at play here: 'GENERATION' (also known as 'song gen'), and 'WORK' (also known as 'finishing the song now'). they are not done with the same rules, nor under the same pretext, nor in the same context, nor at the same time, nor for the same reason. it's almost as if they are not even done by the same person. different floor of the building. different personality type best suited for each of these 2 departments. 'GENERATION' (songgen) procedures and practices: 1. in the best case, the ideas will come to you, not on a songgen session. any other time. music has a spirit of its own, and unfortunately cannot be reliably ordered around. in other words, the truest ideas will come to you at the exact opposite time from when you had planned to find them. For this, you just need to work on your quick-catch techniques. what's the quickest way you can accurately remember the melody/chord/words/etc that just occurred to you, and is it within reach at a moment's notice. handheld audio recording works fine. Handwriting or text works ok, if you have sufficient notation for representing specific melodic/rhythmic/chordal information. 2. specific melodic/rhythmic/chordal information, if it's brand new, by default will not be remembered by you later. that's because, so far, you're the only one who's heard it, and you only heard it once so far. so don't underestimate the importance of documenting the melody, rhythm, and exact words, specifically. the first way you heard it is usually the truest. this is why it's important to catch it and document it. file it into a list and date it. unless you just really don't like it, then whatever, let that one go. 3. besides the lovely surprise of accidental songgen (unplanned, could be rare.... unpredictable, unreliable), you can also do deliberate songgen. In this case, you will deliberately try to make yourself as comfortable as possible (or whatever other mood you prefer) and deliberately start trying to come up with ideas. from anywhere. based on anything, not based on anything. can't come up with any ideas? how about coming up an idea for an idea. etc etc. Don't worry, you won't be actually working on it. no working in the songgen department. save the work for the work department. 4. it's important to remember, on a deliberate songgen session, the first 2 or 3 of a songgen session often are deeply useless and unfilfilling. bad, not good, etc., so don't be alarmed if it seems hopeless to get into it at first. if you can get past these first 2 or 3, it almost always picks up fancifully somewhere among the first 10. you may still feel frustrated that you didn't get enough good ones, but i think you'll find if you do 10 or 20, you'll find that if you look back at them in a day or 2, at least some of them will be just what you always wanted. and again, be prepared also that some of them will not. 5. that's all there is to songgen. no part of the songgen process shall ever be concerned or obligated to finish or produce any of these items. different department, different world. 'work' department: finishing a song, now. wait, hold on, i almost forgot, ????????????which one??????????? and that reminds me of the department that goes in between the 2 departments. 'SELECTION' 1. so, by some other means, you've determined, that at this time in your life you are going to produce a song. now. (in some specified timeframe, or in earnest expedience, whichever is sooner). Which reminds me, this information would have come from the scheduling department or life goals department.... something like that. but for whatever reason, you've become sure beyond the jurisdiction of this departmant ('selection') that you shall now complete and produce a song. you just don't know WHICH one, and that is the job of this department (the selection department). 2. perhaps life is just running so smoothly at the moment that you just happen to know which song you are moved to produce next, and have absolutely no anxiety about whether it's exactly the right choice for you to dedicate the full force and resources of the production departments to it, for however long it takes. perhaps you're in such a carefree mood about this that, despite loving the song enough to choose it, you also have no anxiety about the possibility of screwing it up. in that case, congratulations, your selection is done, and you can move on to the songwriting/work and production departments. 3. in case it's not so easy, you can begin the pre-selection. Go through the entire list of everything you have. anything that puts you in a good mood, add it to the selection list (this will be a temporary list, that only applies to this selection process this time.) 4. you may find yourself thinking defensively. thinking categorically you think you don't want to produce a song at X tempo, or in X type of keycenter, or with X subject matter, ....... or maybe you're trying obsessively avoid the details you did on the last song.... maybe you're avoiding things that accidentally seem to reference current events in ways you didn't intend. etc etc. In some ways, i guess defensive thinking can be good. i mean you probably don't want to produce 2 songs in a row with the same title. (but... actually.... why not?) or 2 in a row at the exact same tempo, or..... something. But, i think you'll notice as you go through the list, you may go through a 'defensive' spell, and find yourself rejecting almost everything. and then, other times, you may be in a more lighthearted mood, and find yourself accepting almost everything. So, i'd suggest, try to think more along the lines of "anything in this list is guaranteed to either be already good, or, be able to be made good." and that's simply true, even in actual garbage cans. 5. Once you complete this list, here's where you have 2 options going forward. go straight to brute random selection, or do one more round through the pre-selection to 'prepare for brute random selection.' 6. if you choose to go through the pre-selection again, here's the thing to beware of: don't do it defensively. don't "narrow it down". You will eliminate everything, and be confused and have to start over. If you go around again, adhere as much as you can to the golden rule of "ANY of these can be made to be the best choice, IF"... and for each one, remember that any of them can work, and ask yourself what would the thing be to make this one work. And often this will lead you accidentally to a small bit of additional writing/arranging/decision on it, and THEN, hopefully you will have that one feeling nice and hot to add to the final random-ready list, and i'd say try to get this final list up to at least 4 items, by the same 'what would it take' question, and that should hopefully get you a small handful of items which would have some brand new details on them, made during this selection process, and hopefully by now you should have such raving desire to do all of them that your biggest dread will actually be that most of these will not be selected. 7. on the other hand, if you are feeling like you just can't get away from the defensive thinking, and your mood is not the greatest, then you are always invited to jump to brute random selection, IMMEDIATELY after that first round of pre-selection. don't even look at them. just count them up, input the quantity, and get your answer. and that is the selection. After all, these all made it to pre-selection, so you're fine. The only reason i no longer recommend a full brute random selection from the entire list (no pre-selection) is because, well........ put it this way, ... it's probably possible for the timing to be just too bad. like let's say there's a guy named .. i dunno.. 'Sam' who is currently all over the news for .... something bad, let's say. doing crimes, or something. etc etc. Like, maybe this week in the news let's say there's a real bad guy in the news named Sam. Well, and let's say you happen to have a song in your list called "i really like Sam, he's a good guy and he's friends with me." written years ago, about a totally different Sam (a nice Sam) before anyone had heard of the bad Sam guy. The pre-selection is mostly just to prevent you from doing that Sam song that particular week. 8. also, after you get your selection, if you wake up the next morning and suddenly feel like the selection is all wrong, don't worry. it's gonna be fine, as long as you know you followed your selection procedure to the best of your ability at the time the 'WORK' department (when you are tasked to finish writing, and produce, the selected song, in the alotted time, or in earnest expedience, whichever is quicker). 1. do you trust the selection (are you convinced that this is the song to be writing right now, to produce next)... just kidding, if you don't trust the selection by now then that means your selection process is faulty and you might as well spiral into a tailspin of confusion. but the selection is fine, because all selections are technically going to be fine 2. have you written the beginning yet 3. if not, figure out what can go at the beginning 4. if you have written the beginning, figure out what goes next 5. if the first part you came up with was not the beginning, and if you now have a beginning but it does not yet connect to the other part you had first, well then you've got yourself a fun puzzle 6. out of what you've written so far, find out how much consecutive material you can accept, starting from the beginning. if it becomes unacceptable to you at any point, then the point just before it became unacceptable is known as the split point 7. continue coming up with the next part after the split point, and don't forget to at least partially consider that at each moment the next right move could be to end it. try to keep an open mind about both ending and non-ending solutions, categorically, in each moment 8. the best time you'll really know what's what, is on a clean run-through. this is when you play through the song, in real time, basically simulating how it will feel for someone to hear it, from the beginning. The effectiveness of these runthroughs at generating the truest genuine songwriting results will mostly depend on how much time has recently elapsed with you NOT hearing the song. i know this has very counterproductive implications 9. if you've re-written a part more than 4 times, you might be cursed for the moment, and the truest thing by default here should be to go with version 1, (and being prepared to hate it, temporarily). the only other real solution here is to spend an extra long amount of time without hearing the song. 10. if time is limited and you don't have time to spend away from the song, try submerging your face in ice cold water and then returning to work. you'll forget what was wrong

ques: How did you figure out the model and animation for the sliding door in the most recent video?
answ: the location of the panels is spaced out linearly, between their start and end points, but the hardest part was figuring out the rotation. according to my reasoning, it needed to be a relationship between the hypotenuse and leg of a right triangle, where the leg grows linearly and the hyponenuse stays constant. so therefore i knew i needed a trigonomic function, so i shopped around and found that acos gave me what i needed. Unfortunately this still isn't really the most authentic result, because the door would have to be spring loaded for it to look like this. What i was originally looking for was something where the first panel moves until it mostly unfolds and then the next panel moves, etc, and i know it's possible to do this but i think it would venture further into calculus than i was ready for at the time

ques: do the colors on the juggling stick things in "out to lunch" have any meaning or are they just colors
answ: i almost wanted them to be the same color, but the reason it's important that they are different colors is because this is an animation (not real) so it's technically more powerful to prove that there are actually 3 clubs. Otherwise it might feel like the animation loop is only 1/3 of the length it actually is. it's important to see the individual clubs changing hands. I made the juggling animation first, and i had 3 different colors just so i could tell them apart. Then i modeled the rooms and did the rest of the animation. Then i had to deal with whether the colors looked good with the scene. There are several moments where 1 club is featured (thrown into the ceiling tile, or onto the light, or when the last 2 go up to the atrium.) So i needed to find a color scheme which looked good with all 3 together, and, also looked good when the individual ones are featured. And switching the clubs at that point was out of the question. so i had to juggle the colors around a bit to make all the scenes look good with the same color scheme. That is generally the meaning of colors: how they look, and how the look feels. And with 3 different but consistent interchanging items, that became somewhat of a puzzle for me

ques: what is the little roll into a snare hit called?
What is a good way to imitate that purely with midi and samples?
answ: it might be called a "ruff"

well, one way is to just get a recording (sample) of someone actually playing that. but the problem there is, it's not very 'playable' for you because you won't have good control over when the final attack is. so if you want something usable, you'll want a steady sample of a continuous drum roll, with fast attack and fast release, so it starts and stops immediately when you press or lift the key, and then you'll want a separate sample, on another key, for a normal snare hit. and then you can play both keys to time the ruffs any way you want. And of course, for decent results, you'll want to make them both dynamic sensitive, and have many different versions of the sample, for different loudness levels, and also many different versions for the same loudness level, so they don't all sound identical

ques: im trying to organize a few hundred sounds by "type", and ive got all the "percussive" stuff on in pile (where the pitch doesn't matter) but i'm not sure what the call the other pile, any good names for non-percussive musical sounds? (pianos, guitars, horns, synths, basses)
answ: besides drums and perc, the 3 categories i use are 'BASS', 'VOC', and 'NON'. bass means bass, voc means my voice, and non means anything besides voc bass drums or perc. These are the functional categories i use for mixing, and for that purpose the category devisions are nearly rock solid. Within the non, there's always a vague attempt to find some categories for arrangement purposes, but the lines always get blurred and break down and argue about how specific to be or not. lead, pno, rhodes, organ, bell, guit, strings, twinkle, pluck, pad, flute, syn, horn, trumpet, miscnon, ..... as you can see there would be a lot of overlap and many things can be used for both, so there never seems to be clarity on that level. i've noticed the same thing when trying to deal with the categorization of my website. at a certain point you just have to accept that real life ultimately will resist total categorization, yet always seems to invite you to try

ques: Why did the orange shirt guy duck under the sign
answ: logistically, that was the only solution i could come up with to get to the right place at the right time. this is one of those puzzles that turns up when you actually get to the set. purple character climbs straight down and looks at the sign. orange character needs to immediately get to a vantage point of looking across the storefronts, while saying the next line. there are many 'bad' ways to do this. orange could climb down and walk directly through purple's line of sight.... this would seem to break purple's concentration. if orange climbs down and walks forward and around back of purple, this goes in between purple and the camera, which is distracting. another possibility is that orange could sort of slide to the side, on the sign, before jumping down. but that seems cumbersome and pointless. i also considered having orange jump off the back of the sign. but it would happen so quickly, i decided that that would look too much like accidental fall. climbing under the sign seemed to be the best way to solve all of this. with the added bonus that maybe he found the extra 'R' letters in the bushes there, under the sign

ques: could you elaborate on the 'dos and donts of speech bubble placement'?
answ: sure. when the camera is very far away, obviously the speech bubble needs to be huge in the scene, in order to be a reasonable size on screen. And it needs to point directly to the characters. but the problem that sometimes happens is, there might be a tree or something closer to the camera than the character, which occupies the screenspace where the speech bubble goes. so if you put the speech bubble in the right place on the screen, it will either be partially obscured by the tree, or, it will disobey the laws of occlusion and be in front of the tree when it shouldn't be. I discovered that, if the camera is totally still, in most cases, you can get away with this. in other words, you can put a speech bubble which appears to point to the character on the 2D screenspace, even if its 3D placement would be impossible. in reality, it's actually a much smaller speech bubble, much closer to the camera, and its position is adjusted so it looks like it points to the character, even though if it were actually next to the character it would be behind the tree. So i've learned that you can usually get away with that when the camera is totally still. But when the camera is slightly moving, this absolutely does not work. There is a shot in the most recent video where the camera is across the street, looking toward the characters through the trees. To put the speech bubble actually next to the characters, it would be entirely obscured by the trees. If i cheat the speech bubble and put it in front of the trees, but smaller, this is a disaster because the camera is drifting slightly, and it becomes glaringly obvious that the bubble is much closer to the camera. So i tried to linearly keyframe the speech bubble to stay positioned next to the character, in 2D screen space. This is an even bigger disaster, and it looks like the scene is broken because the bubble is behaving as if it should be behind the tree, but it actually obscures the tree. Then i tried it with the speech bubble in the same place, but a longer stem reaching mostly back away from the camera toward the character. again, with the drifting camera, as the shape of the speech bubble is revealed, it looks truly bizarre. i ended up having place the bubble far off to the right, outside the trees, and make a very long tail on the 2D plane. which looks a little ridiculous and i didn't really want to do it that way, but i tried absolutely every other way, and it's the only thing that seemed to work. And i've also seen it done in comic books, so it's probably the best way

ques: is your screenwriting process very linear, or do your scripts go through multiple passes?

(person has looked at the caption, to his upper right) 2. damn, 3. phone: 'have you tried going on the internet'? what informs these decisions?

Quite often, and i'm not proud of this, quite often i notice after i've finished producing a video, if i look back at the script there are various nuances that just got forgotten. Usually that's because once i've recorded the audio for the vocal, i don't check the script again. perhaps i should. Or, maybe, in this case, it might be the result of the fact that i went with a full-screen separate card for that announcement, so it wouldn't make any sense to have the character look at it. ques: how about a blur effect when your characters and 3d objects move at really fast speeds?
answ: i can't think of a way to feasibly achieve that. i put some thought about it when i did the scene with the all the cars rushing by. the basic idea that comes to mind is, for that scene, i'd have to speed up the frame rate to about 10,000 times what it normally would be. and then i'd have to composite each final frame (at normal frame rate) to be a blend of the 5000 frames before and after it. i'd be willing to do that, but it would probably take several years just to do one shot. even if the whole process were completely automated, it would still take an absurdly long time even on a supercomputer. so for that reason, that method is out of the question. i also did some thinking about what other gimmicks i can do artistically to sort of give an impression of that effect. and i didn't really have any bright ideas about it, but what i decided to do first is just render the cars moving without blur and take a look at it. i actually thought it looked great without the blur, so i didn't have to worry about adding the blur. and of course, in that shot, i'm glad there's no blur because this way you can actually see the cars in detail

ques: what is that song you made about soft clothing about actually?

ques: Could you share your rules of capital letter usage?
answ: it's not perfectly defined, but some of the general principles are: chord symbols are always capitalized (except for "b" when it's used to mean "flat"). Acronyms are almost always capitalized. the letter L is often capitalized whenever it would otherwise be in danger of being confused for I or 1. the letter "i" when referrring to self is never capitalized. the start of sentences may occasionally need to be capitalized if i feel there is a tone change, or if there should be a decisive break in between sentences, OR if there seems to be a lot of other punctuation in the area and it would otherwise be unclear that it's the start of a new sentence. It's used for emphasis, the same way bold would be used, and the reason i prefer capitals instead of bold is because it's much more likely that the capitals will actually show up on any device, where as bold might get lost somehow. And also if i'm just simply referring to the letter itself, such as the letter F, it is most often capitalized, because that is probably the way that most people think of individual letters. The exception to that, of course, would be the letter "i", which, again, for similar reasons to why L sometimes gets capitalized more often, "i" should be capitalized less often because, similarly, it runs the risk of being confused with l or 1. I also often use capitalization for signage, especially with short contents, such as "STOP" or "EXIT", especially when i am trying to replicate signage that people are familiar with in the outside world

ques: thoughts on 6/4 time? someone told me no one makes songs in 6/4
answ: a lot of people do it without knowing it. they'll put 3/4 on the page and have tiny bars when it really might have been better to say 6/4. there's no reason 'we wish you a merry christmas', 'happy birthday', 'you make me feel like a natural woman', and trillions of other popular songs from every generation wouldn't really be better off saying 6/4 on the page. or, depending on the tempo, be converted to 6/8 or even written as 4/4 and put everything in triplets. a lot of different notation options for songs in 3-feels. But songs with a 4-feel tend to just use 4/4 because it's all groups of 4 within groups of 4 within groups of 4, so 4/4 will always fit. I'd say about 20% of songs use some kind of 3-feel, and within that you're going to have a million different ways of writing the same thing. so those time signatures (6/4, 6/8, etc) would appear less common, but they are used for the same type of music which again i'd say comprises at least 10% of music from all generations

ques: 1.16.23 5:41 pm I wasn't the original asker of this question...but do you think in these types of situations, the time sig is just about what is easiest to write/read on a page?
Or is there a feel difference? Like, as a drummer, would you play differently for a song that was notated as 3/4 vs 6/4?
answ: sure. although a lot of people make weird choices........ 3/4 is more popular but that usually makes the bars tiny (depending on the tempo). because most songs with a 3-feel have the little beats going by at a much faster tempo than quarter notes would usually be. on the other hand, if you consider the whole group of 3 as one beat, you can use 4/4 and put the whole thing in triplets. but that would actually make the bars 4 times longer. possibly too long. in these situations where 3/4 is too tiny and 4/4 with triplets is too long, i usually go with 6/8, which keeps the note values at about the speed you'd expect them to be, and it keeps the bar size at a comfortable speed of about 2 or 3 seconds per bar, as it probably would be in most 4/4 songs

ques: so let's say you have a the number 0.444444444 repeating infinitely. infinitely EXCEPT you're told that the number 5 MIGHT be in the digits somewhere. you don't know if the number 5 is anywhere in there, but you have to completely round it to the nearest whole number.
if there's a 5 somewhere in there, then all the 4s before it correct to a 5 and it ends up rounding to a 1.
but if there isn't, the 4s remain and it rounds to a 0. you don't have infinite time to check for the 5. what do you round it to, 0 or 1?
answ: what?
what?

clearly 0. there's no reason to round it to 1 unless you are following some bizzaro rounding rules. the number is significantly closer to 1, no matter what. .44445, .445, .45, heck even .4999999 are unambiguously closer to 1. the only way that .4444444444445 could possibly end up as 1 is if the number is being rounded 1 digit at a time, over and over again, destructively. and if that happens then the process needs to be fixed because that's a serious corruption. rounding the entire number at once, it unquestionably goes down. there's no rule in the world that says even .45 should go to one, any more than 45 should go to 100. again, the only way 45 goes to 100 is if one person rounded 45 to 50 and then handed it off to someone else without telling them that it came from 45 and then that second person took the new 50 and rounded it to 100. in which case, again, there is a serious communication breakdown here which is corrupting the results and should be investigated

ques: I accidentally came up with a super cool melody with awesome chords... but no lyrics. What do you recommend I do here? I worry that anything I come up with will feel forced
answ: it's there. if the melody and chords really are super cool, then there is a lyricized version that does work. there are a few tricks to help hone in on it. gather the tiny details that you think you know, or almost know. For example: maybe you know a certain word works really well for part of it, for example let's say the word 'banana' just sounds perfect for the last part of it. Or, maybe you know banana sounds great for that part but you doubt it should be about bananas. Add that factoid to your list of factoids, regardless. write down that you love the word banana at the end but you're not sure if it could work. See if you can hone in on any other things you know, about other tiny parts of it. What can you rule out? what can you rule in? Here's another exercise: just start coming up with as many phoenecically functional things as possible that fit, without regard for what you want it to mean. This will help you notice things: for example you might notice that 80% of the results are phrased as a question. You may notice that these 2 little notes there are always either "in the" or "and it". You may notice that certain phrases keep fitting a certain part, over and over. Now, on the other side of the coin, here's a totally different exercise to try: paraphrase the whole feeling of it, without the melody. so just write down, in as many words as you like, what you think the melody is saying, without worrying about how many words or syllables you use. anything you can grasp onto. maybe you think it has a feeling of freshness. maybe you think it has a feeling of 'morning'. maybe you think it has a feeling of sorrow. maybe you think it has a feeling of good news. write down as much as you can about what you think the melody feels like. Then, maybe certain key words will pop out at you that possibly DO fit. And most importantly, regardless of whether any of this works, going through all this makes it much more likely that the answer will actually just fall on your head later when you're not even thinking about it

ques: if i wanted to improve my improvisation and/or songwriting, would it be useful to learn a new chord every day and see how it feels when played after/before/between/instead of other chords?
answ: no. i think doing this will trick you into becoming very uninspired, because a chord includes everything about how/when/where it was used, in the actual song or piece of music. And there's infinite hows/whens/wheres. and each of those things makes everything different about what the chord does. so what i'm saying is, you'll never be able to get a list of all those. So if you say you're gonna "learn a chord" every day, that implies that you're going to be getting them from some list, but there is no list. because it's infinite and there's no order. and some of them are the same, but all of them are the same and different from each other at the same time. Anyway, my point is, the only way to get chords is to either find them how they've already been used in music you know in love, or make them up entirely. so if you're doing it that way, then i think it could be cool. Anyway, for your situation i think i'd recommend 2 different things: 1 is songs/music. just study all the songs/music you actually know and love, and see what they're doing with chords. i think right now you might be expecting it to look like a shelf full of a cereal boxes, lined up like soldiers. but it's really not like that at all, and it's much more like a room full of furniture. that's the best way i can describe it. so if you're learning 1 "piece" of furniture per day, it's gonna be hard enough just to figure out what counts as 1 piece and what counts as 5. or what counts as just the space between the other furniture. anyway, i think you'll see what i mean once you dive into all your favorite songs. and there's another thing i would suggest, that's totally the opposite of studying songs. Just spend some separate time just going nuts on the instrument with a total blank canvas and no song or anything, total free time, next to an open window, and just let the demons fly right in. this is where you make up your own way of doing things. your own way of spending time, on the instrument. Just act like you're sitting in a giant barrel of untapped TIME. time to play any note, not play any note, or combination, for as long or not long as you can imagine. sometimes when doing this, using the pitch bend a little bit can be insanely helpful. just playing notes and tweaking the bend up and down by very small amounts while you play, can be an amazing way to cheat your way into that magic zone of actually feeling like you've just played exactly what you meant to play. and then that supercharges you into very quickly and genuinely discovering all kinds of relationships/intervals/shapes. maybe because it unearths the pitches just enough from their *absolute* location and then suddenly the relationships come alive and become way more potent. It's kind of like when you're eating a cake and you're not sure whether you're tasting the cake or just tasting the cake's location. then you move the cake 3 inches to the left and try the cake again, suddenly you have a more keen awareness of what the cake tastes like, regardless of its location

ques: (in C Lydian) the notes played together are C, E, and F#. what do you call this chord? it can't be C(b5)
because F# is the fourth of Lydian and not the fifth, and because i can add a G right next to the F# and i'll be damned if that G is an Abb
answ: sure it can

i suppose you have a choice: Cmaj(b5), and i promise you there is nothing illegal about calling it that. it happens normally in the real world. (and you can still use F# on the staff in the melody if it goes there). Or, if you insist on preserving the "#4" aspect in the chord symbol, you can say Cmaj(add#4,no5). Although i guarantee if you use the second choice on a chart and give it to a player, you are much much more likely to get a pause and confused looks on the first runthrough. where as if you use Cmaj(b5) it increases the chances significantly that they will actually play what you wanted, the first time through. Sure, it's nice to adhere to proper scale numbering / good enharmonics when you can, but sooner or later you run into edge cases where you have to submit to F#=Gb. There are many more extreme cases, but this is an important one that seems to hit home for you

all the information is relevant. For example: you say you tend to hear it as a loop. Ok, so, ..... is that good or bad? Is there any reason why you feel it should not be a loop? Do you not like the way it feels as a loop? Many great songs indeed are viable as a loop. So i'd say, be open to the possibility of a loop (unless you hate it.) Actually i should be more specific.... when you say loop, are you saying absolutely everything repeats? or are you saying like just the chords and certain things loop? Many songs have a loop but they still use different melodies for cho and verse, or something. On the other hand, there's probably other songs that actually just about use the same melody for both...... anyway, my point is, all the information you can gather from your impressions after the run through is valid, and should be considered. So in this case, your impression is that it seems to loop. Consider the possibility of making it loop. If not the whole thing exactly, then consider the possibility of keeping the same form / chords and then just raising or lowering the energy. in most loop based songs, the raise and lower of energy is the bread and butter that takes you from verse to chorus to verse

you might get some more wisdom over time, but i feel like nothing is ever going to fully shield you from this dread zone of 'trying too hard' and 'thinking too much.' And i'm not blaming you. The reason you are thinking and trying is because you really care about this damn thing, and rightfully so. But the weird thing about music is it really clams up when people start trying and thinking a lot. It wants to find you, so be aware that it will find you. you just don't always get to decide when. But until then, just recognize all the information you are getting, which, in this case, is that it seems to require a loop. ques: what the fuck is a time signature and how do i read and write their expressions
answ: i guess 90% of the game here is realizing that the most common time signature is 4/4, also sometimes written as 'C'. This means there are 4 beats per bar. if you already have an understanding of beats and bars, then i can go ahead and explain how the number system works (which, again, is really only important about 10% of the time, because most of the time it's just 4/4 and you don't have to worry about it). But if you don't know what beats and bars are, then i'd have to start there. There is a mathematical explanation of how the time-signature system works, and it's good to understand that, but, there's also some ways that it's used that are more like a societal standard and not so much just math. The way the number system is supposed to work is, the top number is how many beats there are in a bar (4) and the bottom number is what note gets one beat. So for example, 4/4 (written on paper with the first number directly on top of the second number) means there's 4 beats per bar, and a quarter note gets one beat. 7/8 should mean there are 7 beats per bar, and an 8th note gets one beat. But actually, the second half of those statements is kind of shaky, because, for example, in a time signature like 6/8, which is extremely common, it would be like "6 beats per bar, and an 8th note gets 1 beat" but in many cases 6/8 is really felt more like 2 beats per bar and a dotted quarter gets one beat (which is mathematically equivalent, but no one writes dots in timesignatures). But, one thing that remains certain, it still correctly describes the bar length. So it would always be accurate to say, for 6/8 for example, there are 6 8th notes per bar. In 4/4, there are 4 quarter notes per bar. in 11/16, there are 11 16th notes per bar. This way of describing it will always be correct. in 3/4, there are 3 quarter notes per bar. in 2/2, there are two half notes per bar

ques: what were the origins of "where I've been"?
answ: during an idea generating session on apr 11, 2019, i came up with the chord figure and melody for the verse. during a songwork session on apr 20, 2021, i got the lyrics to the first stanza. in late august 2022, i was searching through the list to find the next song to select for song/video production (due sept 13), and "where i've been" seemed to be a highly favored choice at that time, but i instead decided to actually use no selection, and just start writing a video (to possibly lead into a song, or maybe not) without any song selection. But i guess "where i've been" was still at the forefront of my mind, so i ended up launching into it within the first few seconds of the dialogue. It was actually my goal to really write something that combined song and non-song in a more 50/50 balanced way, but then there's also generally a desire to make the song playable as a song on its own, outside the video. As i continued writing, i actually broke out of the song and back into more dialogue after the first stanza. And that was pretty fun and cool, but i knew that wouldn't work for the song-only version. So then i found myself in a position where i was writing 2 different versions of this whole thing, in parallel: one version which breaks in and out of song, and another version that stays in the song once the song starts. And pretty quickly i realized that that would be way too confusing. So i just kept it in song without breaking it. So my goal of really mixing the song and non-song 50/50 turned out to be a failure, this time around. and the "where i've been" song ended up taking over, with no return to diaglogue, for the rest of the video. Also, the goodbyes section has a completely alternately written version, which still ends with the last line as is (where i was / wasn't). I ended up completely rewriting that section because the first version felt like it had too strong a similarity to the 'bring me down / pick me up' section of ground plane

I can think of a lot of songs (especially common in old timey songs) that have a chord pattern like: C C7 F F#dim C A7 D7 G7 C A7 D7 G7 C But it still feels and sounds like C major even though most of those chords aren't in the key. Would you still consider that to be in C major?

answ: indeed, i call that 'normal'

that one you just mentioned reminds me of a door handle that turns sideways when the door opens. even though the handle is normally not in that position, the sideways position IS actually a normal position for the purpose of opening the door. not only normal, but powerful. a real door opener, that C7 (to F)
yep

ques: what is the inspiration for la de da de da de da de day oh? i feel like it has a lot more hidden meaning than some of your other songs.
answ: the verse part was written somewhere in early 2009 when i was feeling like there's too many zillions of ways to do songwriting and i haven't even discovered most of them yet. so i was feeling like i don't have enough time to do stuff. the "be like you" is just a lyric swap i did when i picked it up to work on it in sept 2012. it just felt more 'in the pocket' musically. and 'believe them too' was from the same 2012 session, to match 'be like you' in that same pocket. prior to the sept 2012 session, i only had up to the end of the first pre-chorus, which is about 'wanting to write a song'. and it was all cued up to hit the chorus. so 'la de da de da' is like, that's the sound of a song being written. i got the entire chorus written on that session, and i was pleased with the results. that possibly made the song feel like it was up on a pedestal (afraid to touch it because i like it too much, i'm afraid i'll ruin it). and it stayed right there for years, with nothing beyond the first cho. it finally was up for selection in october 2017 when i was brave enough, and it was picked by the final random selection among about 27 other semi-final choices. i almost changed my mind the next day because i was still afraid to ruin it, but then i suddenly tricked myself into imagining the second verse, then the first 3 lines of the second verse came very quickly and then i was confident in the song selection. i continued the writing until the end, according to my standard songwriting practices and procedures

ques: i never really tried to comprehend music as a kid so i developed absolute pitch and relied solely on that and now i still have bad relative pitch. for example in choir if the sheet music is in a different key from what we're actually singing in, i get really slow at reading the music. how can i stop thinking about absolute pitch to get more fluent at relative pitch which i know is the actually important one? also i hate when people think having absolute pitch equals talent, but then i'm still happy that i get to annoy my friends by naming the pitch of the microwave or the car honk or something,

ques: i started making music while i was depressed, and the results are music that sounds like you would expect a depressed person to make (depressing), but i never released it. i feel better now, but i'm wondering if i should even bother finishing and releasing, or if i should just focus on making new music?

finishing the old stuff will get stuff out faster, but working on new stuff will make my body of released work happier, on average (100%). i'm wondering how much that matters, or whether i am overthinking.

idunno, maybe releasing the older stuff will bring me closure, and someone else catharsis. or maybe it will just make others share in my old uncomfy feelings that i've already worked so hard to shed, and heal from. some people only like music that sounds kinda dark, so releasing it might satisfy my libran desire to please everybody, by offering more variety............. do you have any thoughts/feelings about this? have you ever had a similar dilemma?
answ: you can do both, if you can come up with a system you like, for organizing your time
if you find yourself thinking about it, then you might as well figure out a clever system you can really get behind

a number of different activities come to mind: you can write brand new things, and add them to the list. you can select older things on the list, and bring them to your modern writing table and learn how to work on them just as you would work on a modern song, fixing what you don't like. you can use your old songs as practice doing this. Another variation on these sorts of activities is: you can select something from the list and mark that as the item to be completed next (before any other) and then do whatever you gotta do to make it how you like it. The point is, there are so many different variations of workflows here, there's a lot of ways to get confused about which thing and which order you're working on things. I think as long as you're already thinking about this, it's worth really trying to craft a great system that you can really get excited about. in due time it can all be done, to the best of your liking

ques: Haiya bill. Just wondering in the melody, lyrics, chords, tempo, and roadmap, do you ever jot down ideas for specific instrumentation at certain points (brass hits, some guitar / synth figure, etc.)

the first example that comes to mind, to explain this, is not my song, but it's a good example to explain it: if i were writing the song Africa (by Toto), i'd say the huge drum fill just before the chorus, that would be something written into the song. because that's something that takes the lead at that moment. if you were singing that song to a friend, you'd almost certainly have to sing that drum part there. it's a feature. but anyway, here are some examples from my own songs, of things that were written, or not: in "christmas isn't real", no specific instrument parts were written (other than the core elements you listed, as always) in "slow down", the melody riff in between stanzas near the end of the song, was written (it's just about the same as the vocal melody anyway, but it was written that that riff would occur there, instrumentally). The instrumental intro, however, was not written until production time. the instrumental break in the middle of the song was also not written aside from knowing that it would sync generally to the verse roadmap. in "i'm scared" the bassline in the title verses was written. Also the short instrumental riff that occurs midway through the chorus (fallin) section, was written. however i think there's a different variation the second time around which was not planned in the writing in "in california" the instrumental lines in the second prechorus were written. the horn stabs during that time, however, were not. The instrumental riffs behind the vocal during the chorus/bridge ('alright') sections, were not written in "i'm a princess", the instrumental melody in the chorus (which is the section that begins after 'about my world') was written. however, the much crazier melody in the final 8 bars was not written, aside from the road map and all the other core elements that you mentioned (as always) in "meet me in september", the instrumental (and vocal) riff after "celebrate"/"complicated" was written. also the instrumental fill between that section and the following verse, was written (both the first and second times that occurs). Also the climbing instrumental riff in the 3rd and 4th bars of one of the middle verses, was written the bell melody in the outtro of "movie star" was not written. also in the writing that was assumed to be a fade out in "i'm best friends with my own front door", in the break after the first verse-stanza, the instrumental repeat of the melody was written in "where i've been", the low-B bass rhythms near the end (during the 'good times' section) were written

ques: You said something interesting about how you can describe music as having three elements (melody, chord, lyric). At first I thought that including lyric in those three was a little silly but then I realized that that actually makes complete sense.

Theres a very real extent to which the sound of a lyric or the context of a lyric affects the song itself or the way the song feels. game music can reach higher heights than a lot of other music. because one of those core elements is actually YOU and what you are doing in the game. this is a perfect example of music and non-music enhancing each other intimately
no reason it can't be lyricless, for a game or movie score. the game scene/action is what takes the focus, instead of the language in the lyric of a song

ques: can you explain your process for mentally figuring out the hex codes for colors again? i remember seeing your explanation for it once before a few years ago but have since forgotten it
answ: it's R G B. the first 2 digits are red, the middle two are green, the last two are blue. And each of these 3 sections runs on a scale from 00 to FF, in hexidecimal that means 0 to 16, with 00 being the lowest and FF being the highest. So if you know how to mix RGB then you're all set. bright red is FF0000. bright green is 00FF00. pure blue is 0000FF. black is 000000. white is FFFFFF. medium grey is like 888888. bright magenta is FF00FF. etc
